newsitem.title: USA: Extremists grow in numbers since Oklahoma city.
newsitem.headline: Extremists grow in numbers since Oklahoma city.

text.p: In the nearly two years since the Oklahoma City bombing, right-wing extremists have continued to flourish in the United States, setting up their own courts and filing scores of false liens against government officials in what critics call acts of "paper terrorism."

They have even concocted several new conspiracy theories including claims that the U.S. government kidnaps people in U.N.-style black helicopters and was behind the April 19, 1995, Oklahoma bombing that killed 168 people.

But one thing extremist groups are not doing is hailing Timothy McVeigh, the disgrunted Gulf War veteran accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, as either a hero or a martyr -- at least not yet.

"He's no poster boy. When the militias discuss him it is in terms of his being a pawn but basically they don't even discuss him," said Gail Gans, associate director of research for the Anti-Defamation League, which monitors extremist and hate groups in the United States. "McVeigh evokes mixed feelings within the milita movement because the loss of life at Oklahoma City appalls many people."

McVeigh was to go on trial next Monday in Denver with prosecutors and possibly even his own lawyers reportedly prepared to link him to several extremist groups from militias to the Klu Klux Klan to white supremacist settlements on the Oklahoma-Arkansas border.
Prosecutors, who amassed a great deal of physical evidence linking him to the crime, must show motive, while his lawyers may want to show McVeigh was but a pawn in a wider conspiracy.

CBS News on Monday said McVeigh may have been linked to or inspired by an extremist group called CSA (Covenant, Sword and Arm of the Lord), which it said planned to bomb the Murrah building in 1983 but decided at the last minute not to do so.

Experts on domestic extremism said there has been no dearth of violent or attempted violent incidents since 1995, ranging from a foiled plot to blow up a key FBI fingerprint centre to the bust-up of a gang of white supremacists responsible for a string of bank robberies in the Middle West.
But the ADL's Gans said that what is also clear is that many militia members have gone underground.

"They now hold small, unadvertised meetings in private homes and no longer publicly identify themselves as militias," she said, adding that many extremists have been publicly active in setting up "common-law" courts that seek to replace the existing legal system with vigilante justice.

The courts, which number more than 125 and are active in 35 states, issue scores of phony legal documents and liens against property, often the property of elected officials, in what extremism experts call a campaign of "paper terrorism."

One county court official in Texas complained that 40 percent of her time was spent dealing with phony liens and other bogus documents and that court officials have been threatened by extremists who refuse to process their claims.

Law enforcement sources said the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms and Tobacco was forced to reassign its agent in charge of a case against three Georgia militiamen when his name, address, phone number and photo wound up on the Internet. His personal details had been lifted from a loan application he filled out at a bank.

Klanwatch, operated by the Southern Poverty Law Centre, said at least 858 extremist groups operated in the United States last year, up 6 percent since 1995, and that they included 380 armed militias. Klanwatch spokesman Richard Baudouin said extremists appeared to be improving their intelligence-gathering networks on public and private targets.

Richard Davis, a lawyer who formerly headed the Treasury Department's law enforcement agencies, said it was clear extremists and their strong anti-government atttitudes have not abated in the past two years. But he added there was more going on under the surface. "It is clear these groups cannot take too much of the spotlight."
